## The Invention of Kindergarten
The term "kindergarten" itself was carefully chosen. Froebel saw children not as blank slates to be filled with knowledge, but as seeds planted in a carefully cultivated garden, with a teacher as the gardener. Just as a gardener understands the nature of each plant and creates conditions for healthy growth, so too must educators understand the developmental nature of each child and provide appropriate conditions for learning. This horticultural metaphor was not merely poetic; it expressed Froebel's core belief that education must be consonant with natural human development.

Friedrich Fröbel fue un pedagogo alemán que cambió la forma de educar a los niños pequeños. Nació el 21 de abril de 1782 en Oberweissbach, Alemania.
Fröbel creía que los niños no son adultos pequeños, sino seres que aprenden mejor cuando juegan, exploran y están en contacto con la naturaleza.
Por eso, en 1840 fundó en Alemania el primer "Kindergarten", que significa "jardín de niños". Lo llamó así porque pensaba que los niños son como plantas: necesitan cuidado, un buen ambiente y libertad para crecer a su ritmo. El maestro sería como el jardinero que los acompaña.
Inventó materiales educativos que llamó "dones": pelotas de lana, cubos, cilindros y figuras de madera. Con ellos, los niños aprendían matemáticas, arte y cómo funciona el mundo mientras jugaban. También incluyó canciones, rondas, huertos y actividades con las manos. Todo buscaba desarrollar el cuerpo, la mente y el corazón por igual.
Al principio, sus ideas fueron criticadas y hasta prohibieron los Kindergarten en Prusia. Pero su trabajo inspiró a educadores de todo el mundo. Gracias a él, hoy la educación preescolar se basa en el juego, la creatividad y el respeto por la infancia.

Friedrich Wilhelm August Fröbel (1782-1852) war ein deutscher Pädagoge, der als Begründer des Kindergartens und der modernen Vorschulpädagogik gilt. Fröbel wurde am 21. April 1782 in Oberweißbach, Thüringen, geboren und wuchs unter schwierigen familiären Verhältnissen auf.
Fröbels Bildungskarriere begann in Jena, wo er Naturwissenschaften und Mathematik studierte.
1817 gründete Fröbel in Griesheim und später in Keilhau eine eigene Schule, das „Allgemeine Deutsche Erziehungsanstalt“. Seine pädagogischen Ansätze basierten auf der Überzeugung, dass Kinder durch Selbsttätigkeit und kreatives Spielen am besten lernen. Er sah das Spiel als die höchste Ausdrucksform kindlicher Entwicklung und Kreativität an und entwickelte spezielle Spielmaterialien, die sogenannten „Fröbelgaben“. Diese bestanden aus einfachen geometrischen Formen und wurden dazu verwendet, Kindern grundlegende Konzepte der Mathematik und des räumlichen Denkens zu vermitteln.
Im Jahr 1837 gründete Fröbel den ersten Kindergarten in Bad Blankenburg. Der Begriff „Kindergarten“ verdeutlicht seine Vorstellung, dass Kinder wie Pflanzen in einem Garten gepflegt und gefördert werden sollten, um ihr volles Potenzial zu entfalten. Fröbel betonte die Bedeutung von Spiel, Musik, Handarbeit und Naturbeobachtung in der frühkindlichen Erziehung. Overview

In English, too, the kindergarten goes by its German name. The German word Kindergarten means “garden (Garten) of children (Kinder).” It has been taken into many languages, English among them.
The name was coined by the German educator Friedrich Froebel (Fröbel, 1782–1852). In 1840, in the small town of Bad Blankenburg in Thuringia, he gave this name to an institution for young children. In Japan, too, the first kindergartens were modeled on Froebel’s. ## History

From an institution for play and activity

Froebel was born in 1782 in Oberweißbach in Thuringia. He visited the Swiss educator Pestalozzi to learn from him, and from 1816 he ran a school where he taught children. In 1826 he published his main work, The Education of Man.

## Fröbel and the First Kindergarten: The Invention of Play-Based Education in History and Research

*The kindergarten is now so universal an institution that it is easy to forget it was invented — by one man, Friedrich Fröbel (1782–1852), in the small Thuringian town of Bad Blankenburg in 1837. This review traces the origins of the first kindergarten and its remarkable curriculum of play: the Gifts, the Occupations, the mother-songs, and the garden itself. It follows the movement through its suppression in Prussia, its diffusion across the Atlantic by a network of pioneering women, and its eventual transformation inside public school systems. It then asks how Fröbel's founding claim — that play is the serious work of early childhood — has fared in modern developmental science. Contemporary research on guided play, block construction, and spatial-mathematical development offers striking, though not unqualified, support for practices Fröbel designed nearly two centuries ago, while historical scholarship complicates both the movement's saintly image and the popular legend of its influence on modern art and architecture. The review closes with practical implications for families and early educators.*

The German term *Kindergarten *is widely recognized and understood, but the name of the man who coined the term, ultimately redefining early education, has largely been forgotten. In fact, today, the name Friedrich Froebel is hardly known even in educational circles. However, the foundations laid by this 19th century German educator still firmly underlie early childhood education.

What we have come to know as the hallmarks of childhood were established by Froebel over 175 years ago. At that time, play was viewed as idle, and children were considered miniature adults. Froebel radically asserted that children learn best through play, that academics should be left for after the age of seven, and that children need to be in an environment suited to learning through their hands. He believed that a child naturally loves movement, music, and exploration in nature. Stories and rhymes should be the basis for later letter and number skills.

Froebel did not so much invent these key factors of childhood, rather, he brought them to the surface and into everyone’s attention. Froebel made children important. His ideas became embodied in his original “Kindergarten” or a “Children’s Garden” based on the philosophy that children, like plants, grow at their own pace but must be nurtured by the family and society.
